thread.title: S&P 500 Weekly Update: Headlines Rule The Market, Don't Panic Over The 'Crisis' Of The Day

author: Fear & Greed Trader
title: S&P 500 Weekly Update: Headlines Rule The Market, Don't Panic Over The 'Crisis' Of The Day
text:
"Investing is the intersection of economics and psychology." - Seth Klarman
The investing backdrop may not be as good as many would like to see it, but while things are far from perfect, they're not bad either. The results of all these on again off again headlines lately is a market that jerks higher and lower with every news announcement. Then quickly reverses course with the next headline.
During this entire Bull market we have seen how some investors rely on conjecture to form their investment strategy. They say they are following a feeling they have, rather than listening to the message of the market. Time after time we have heard; the stock market is due for a pullback. Then the inevitable words; surely after these gains and a new high, a serious market pullback is inevitable. Then when the market consolidates, it's common to hear: the top is in, the indices look like they are rolling over.
The problem with that line of thinking is the data doesn't support any of that commentary. It is pure speculation. Instead the message here has been Strength begets strength. Why? Because that is what occurs in a secular bull market, and it isn't conjecture, or a feeling , it is fact. There is no rule or law that says a new high can't be followed by another new high. That a round of market strength can't continue. Guess what, that is exactly what has occurred. This pause in the bull run is just that, a pause.
Many still don't see it that way. The reason none of that sounds logical is because we let emotions take over. It's the thought that the odds favor a decline, because all seems so bad around us. Sorry, but they don't. When the equity market makes a big move it is signaling fundamental strength and it is forecasting change. In the case of an uptrend, a change for the better. It is at that time that investors should be interested in equities, not lightening up and raising cash. There is room for improvement, and improvement brings higher equity prices.
That is one of the reasons investors get tripped up and sell at the wrong time. Conversely many decide to buy at the wrong time because they are looking for everything to line up absolutely perfectly. Forget about the absolutes, the equity market does not care about them. A successful investor knows that when all of the market data is looking oh so rosy, that is when it is time to get cautious.
The premise is that it can't get much better, and the market sniffs out the next change. After a long positive run, with all feeling so good, the next change is apt to be negative. The rosy picture that made everyone comfortable and possibly euphoric starts to deteriorate, because things just can't get any better, there are excesses that have built up. What happens next traps a lot of investors. The technical picture deteriorates, the top has been put in, and then the stock market rolls over. With all of the commentary about this or that "crisis," it's perfectly clear we are not in that market environment.
When we look around today, I see investors with the negative mindset that I described earlier. We listen to a lot of folks state they don't trust this rally. Investors tell us they have this feeling . The trade war will crush economic growth, followed by anxiety over interest rates. Then there is the incessant commentary that the stock market is overvalued and it can't go higher.
All of that tells me it is not time to abandon the equity market. The "no one believes" viewpoint fits perfectly with what has happened in the last few years, and in that time period the market has not crashed. It has made new highs. How high the S&P goes from here no one knows, what I do know is the the probability of a dire scenario taking place with this backdrop is very low.
Savvy investors will use this crisis of the day to their advantage, adding not detracting form their equity holdings.
Economy Scott Grannis supplies us with evidence that the economy is grinding higher. The volume of Truck tonnage has had a strong tendency to track equity prices.
Truck tonnage surged 9.5% in the year ending April '18, and the S&P 500 Index is up almost 14% over the same period.
May Dallas Fed Manufacturing index rose 5 points to 26.8 after dipping 1 point to 21.8 in April. It was at 17.3 last May, and as high as 38.4 in February, the best since December 2004.
Markit US Manufacturing PMI was reported right around expectations at 56.4, down fractionally from the April report of 56.5. Chris Williamson, Chief Business Economist at IHS Markit said:
The U.S. manufacturing sector enjoyed another bumper month in May, though continues to run hot. The past two months have seen the strongest back-to-back improvements in order books since the fall of 2014, fueled by strengthening domestic demand. New orders have in fact now grown at a faster rate than output in each of the past five months, highlighting how producers have struggled to boost production to meet sales. In the words of one manufacturer, 'We're selling more than we can make.'
The upturn has stretched supply chains to the extent that May saw the greatest lengthening of delivery times in the near-ten year history of the survey. Producers are also finding it difficult to find suitable staff. With sales growing faster than production, backlogs of work are accumulating at the fastest rate for nearly four years, which should support further production growth in coming months. Business expectations regarding future production in fact picked up again to one of the highest levels seen over the past three years, adding to signs that strong growth will persist through the summer months.
ISM Manufacturing report bounced back nicely in May, rising from 57.3 up to 58.7 and above the consensus forecast for an increase to 58.2. While the index is off of its recent highs, relative to history, it is still at very high levels.
Construction Spending during April 2018 was estimated at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $1.3 billion, 1.8 percent above the revised March estimate of $1.2 billion. During the first four months of this year, construction spending amounted to $387.0 billion, 6.6 percent above the $363.1 billion for the same period in 2017.
Consumer confidence in May rose to 128.0 from a revised 125.6 in April (was 128.7). The present situation component improved to 161.7 from a revised 157.5 (was 159.6). The expectations index was 105.6 compared to 104.3 previously (revised from 108.1).
Nonfarm payrolls increased a solid 223k in May, gains of 159k in April (revised from 164k) and 155k in March (revised from 135k), for a net upward revision of 15k. The unemployment rate fell to 3.8% from 3.9% and is the lowest since late 1969. Average hourly earnings rose 0.3% after edging up 0.1% previously and are up 2.71% y/y versus 2.56% y/y. Hours worked were unchanged at 34.5. The labor force participation rate dipped to 62.7% from 62.8%.
The employment picture remains robust.
April Pending Home Sales Index down -1.3% vs. consensus of 0.4% for the month. As per Lawrence Yun , NAR chief economist:
The housing market this spring is hindered because of the severe housing shortages in much of the country. Pending sales slipped in April and continued to stay within the same narrow range with little signs of breaking out. Feedback from realtors, as well as the underlying sales data, reveal that the demand for buying a home is very robust. Listings are typically going under contract in under a month, and instances of multiple offers are increasingly common and pushing prices higher.
Global Economy OECD released its biannual update of real GDP estimates across the global economy (table). World growth is forecast to come in at 3.82% and 3.93% in 2018 and 2019, respectively, +20 and +34 bps revision from the most recent updated back in November.
JPMorgan Global Manufacturing PMI , was reported at a nine month low in May, coming in at 53.1. The April read was 53.5. As per David Hensley, Director of Global Economic Coordination at JPMorgan:
The May PMI data suggest global manufacturing output growth is holding up well. Output growth is down from the robust pace of 2H17 but it remains solid. Our separate measures of global final goods demand are firming this quarter, supporting output growth. However, the PMI suggests that inventory growth may be decreasing. Such a shift in the mix of demand would be positive for the future.
Eurozone Manufacturing PMI comes was reported at 55.5 in May, down form the April reading of 56.2. As per Chris Williamson, Chief Business Economist at IHS Markit:
The eurozone manufacturing sector reported its weakest expansion for 15 months in May. Some of the weakness may have been related to a higher than usual number of holidays during the month, but risks appear tilted towards growth remaining subdued or even cooling further in coming months.
Slowing export sales have been a key drag on both production and order book growth, with the May survey indicating that new export orders rose at the weakest rate for nearly two years, linked in part to the appreciation of the euro alongside reports of weakened demand for imports from key markets, notably the U.S.
China Manufacturing PMI data was reported at 51.1 in April, little changed from the previous month's figure of 51.0 and above market consensus of 50.9.
China Services PMI rose to 52.9 in April from a four month low of 52.3 in March and beating market consensus of 52.2. New orders rose at a faster pace, employment continued to rise and sentiment improved slightly.
Canada manufacturing PMI rolled in very strong with the highest reading in seven years. The May reading was 56.2, up from the April report of 55.5. As per Tim Moore, Associate Director at survey compilers IHS Markit:
Canadian manufacturers achieved their strongest overall performance since April 2011, with the headline PMI reading boosted by faster new order growth and the greatest increase in pre-production inventories for six years. The combination of rising workloads and increased stock building bodes well for near-term output growth.
A number of survey respondents noted that high levels of capacity utilization had meant that production volumes were insufficient to keep up with incoming new work in May. There were also some reports that supply chain disruptions had acted as a brake on output growth, with constraints on transport capacity commonly cited by manufacturers.
May data highlighted stronger cost pressures across the manufacturing sector, led by rising prices for metals and energy-intensive goods. A combination of higher input costs and robust demand conditions meant that manufacturers increased their output charges to the largest extent for seven years.
Earnings Observations Factset Research Weekly Update:
Earnings Growth: For Q2 2018, the estimated earnings growth rate for the S&P 500 is 18.9%. If 18.9% is the actual growth rate for the quarter, it will mark the second highest earnings growth since Q1 2011 (19.5%).
Valuation: The forward 12-month P/E ratio for the S&P 500 is 16.2. This P/E ratio is equal to the 5-year average (16.2) and above the 10-year average (14.3).
Earnings Scorecard: For Q1 2018 with 98% of the companies in the S&P 500 reporting actual results for the quarter), 77% of S&P 500 companies have reported a positive EPS surprise and 77% have reported a positive sales surprise.
The Political Scene
The initial catalyst for the selling on Tuesday was Italian populist parties in turmoil trying to gradually hammer out an agreement to govern. Proposing to lay out a platform that is both antagonistic towards the EU, promises higher deficits, and proposes a new possible form of financing that in a certain light looks like an alternative currency to the euro.
For Italy, the real concern isn't 10 year debt, but the front end, which has surged to the highest spread over German yields since November of 2013; that said, it's still a tiny fraction of the spreads recorded during the EZ sovereign debt crisis.
Source: Bespoke
The Italian front end is now pricing all sorts of catastrophic tail risk, up to and including eurozone departure. That said, neither of the parties in the new government have a mandate to leave the euro, and their majority is relatively small so any failure of nerve across the party's membership would mean the status quo prevails and create a huge rally in the Italian front end. While there are risks, they remain conditional; this is not the end of the world.
The Fed and Interest Rates In the last month investors have heard their fill of what would happen to stocks with a 10 year at 3%. Then it was the fear of 3.25 and 3.5% that would be right around the next corner.
The 10-year treasury closed the week at 2.89%. The successful investor makes an assessment, allows the situation to develop, then reassess before making any premature changes in strategy.
Sentiment According to AAII , bullish sentiment dropped from 38.6% down to 35.0%. That breaks the streak of three consecutive weeks of increases.
Crude Oil The weekly inventory report showed a decrease of 3.6 million barrels in the past week, partially negating the increase from the previous week. Gasoline inventories rose a negligible 0.5 million barrels. The oil market was mired in mixed trading for the week as it looks for some equilibrium after a nice upside run. WTI closed on Friday at $65.87, down $1.82
The Technical Picture The daily chart highlights the back and forth, up and down activity, as the tug of war between the bulls and bears continues. The index resides right in the middle of the on going corrective phase. About 6% from the old high, and roughly 6% from the February lows.
On Tuesday we saw an intraday low of 2676, so for now we will use that as very short term support level. Resistance stands at the intraday high on May 22, S&P 2742.
The Russell 2000 continues on its march to new highs, a very strong signal that the entire bull market is on solid footing. A simple message signaling the probability of a bear market happening anytime soon is extremely low.
Individual Stocks and Sectors Consumer Staples continues as the worst YTD performer. A sign that institutions are not looking to be involved in a defensive sector. Quite the Opposite for Consumer Disc. (driven by Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN )). Energy took a breather, dropping out as the YTD leader. However, the sector is the leader in Q2, up 10%. Crude Oil is up 13+% for the year. Technology remains resilient and the clear leader once again, up 9% for the year.
Investors who have remained resolute in their bullish strategy are being rewarded. Alibaba ( BABA ) and Apple ( AAPL ) just forged new closing highs. Facebook ( FB ), has come all the way back from the data breach fiasco. The semiconductors are not dead at all, having rallied nicely off the early may lows. Energy has given some of their gains back as WTI weakened, but that trade could just be pausing instead of ending.
Once market participants realize that the trade issue that is being bandied about won't have much effect on the bottom line of many industrial companies, I believe the group rallies.
There are endless opportunities being offered by this bull market. Many stocks are breaking out of trading ranges while we hear about how dire the situation is around us. Listen to the market or listen to the person telling us how Italy will end the bull market. I've made my decision.
It sure doesn't seem possible with all of the turmoil, but the facts are the facts. The S&P was up 2% for the month of May. The NYSE cumulative A/D line made a record high, the Russell 2000 made a record high. This past week there was calamity all around. It started with Italy, then more trade war talk, and North Korea. Despite that the S&P closed the week with a 13 point gain. Nothing to write home about, but one would have thought the bottom would have fallen out of the index. Or at least that is what we were being told was going to happen.
I watched Friday's rally wipe out the small loss the S&P had suffered up until then. On Friday, anyone that had a negative opinion on the global trade issue was rolled out and told us how horrible things were going to get. The S&P rallied 28 points.
The stock market is telling investors something, the question is are you listening? The example shows how the headlines and emotion rule our perception of what is going on.
Investors have seen the S&P 500 in a consolidation phase for most of 2018. These phases have no time limit, so we should be prepared for the eventuality that the market could easily be marking time for a while. The underlying fact remains the long term trend has not been violated. In essence, nothing has changed.
Unless I see a decided change in what the market is telling us now, new highs are very likely to still lie ahead in 2018. Sound crazy with all of the concerns? Remember, this is still a bull market. Italian politics, trade talks, interest rates, North Korea, etc. all have resolutions that will not end the bull market.
When an investor asks about a particular issue that may be bothering them, I usually tell them to first take a look at some of the positives that are around. Sure there are worries, but there are also some good things happening.
Liz Ann Sonders shares a graphic that sums up the trends in the U.S. Economy nicely:
I continue to hold the positive view that we've talked about week after week in the face of a lot of negativity. That view remains centered around not only on the technical level but the fundamental backdrop as well. The economic data is suggesting an improved growth outlook. Solid double-digit earnings growth this year, with expected high single-digit growth next year. Despite the worries, the Federal Reserve will be normalizing interest rates gradually against modest inflationary forces. In my view, valuations are fair to inexpensive.
In my view, all of the negative responses we have seen to any of the issues that are presented to us are wild overreactions. Then again, we may need that to clear out any excesses that may have built up. This is how strong secular bull markets march on. Global Trade isn't going to stop tomorrow, and corporations aren't going to see massive declines in earnings. Let's remember the big lift the tax package delivered.
A gentle reminder: The latest round of earnings also came with one of the strongest guidance readings from CEOs in 17 years. Company managers were well aware of all the tariff talks, yet they stayed positive with solid forward guidance. A CEO has no reason to stick his or her neck out unless they have a real good read on what is happening around them. Apparently what is happening around them is positive.
Another message being delivered. Let others wring their hands over issues that are being made out to be a lot bigger than they really are. Despite all of the issues, the S&P is less than 5% from a new all time high. Keep the situation in perspective and stay the course.
